 You May Qualify for These 7 Programs If You Live on Social Security Alone
 Chris Lewis, CEPF 2026년 11월 7일 토 오전 10:05 UTC 0 
 Social Security was never designed to be a retiree's entire
 income . Yet for millions of older Americans, it is. The average retired
 worker collected $2,071 a month in 2026 after a 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment
 (COLA), according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). That's roughly
 $24,852 a year, before Medicare premiums and taxes take a bite.
 If that sounds like a tight budget, you're not imagining it. The good news is
 that a patchwork of federal and state programs exists specifically to help
 people with limited income and resources cover groceries, Medicare costs,
 prescriptions, utility bills, and housing. None of these programs are automatic
 just because Social Security is your only income. Each has its own rules, and
 eligibility often comes down to exact income and asset limits that vary by
 state. Here's what to know before you apply.
 Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 1. Extra Help with Medicare prescription drug costs
 Extra Help, also called the Low-Income Subsidy, helps cover the cost of Medicare
 Part D prescription drug coverage, including premiums, deductibles, and copays.
 For 2026, the SSA sets the income limit at $23,940 a year for an individual and
 $32,460 for a married couple, with resource limits of $18,090 for an individual
 and $36,100 for a couple. Limits run higher in Alaska and Hawaii. Resources
 counted include money in checking and savings accounts, stocks, and bonds, but
 not your home, car, or burial funds set aside up to $1,500. People who qualify
 get enrolled in a Medicare drug plan where they pay $0 for the premium and
 deductible. You can apply through the SSA or your state Medicaid office.
 Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. 
 2. Medicare Savings Programs for Part A and Part B costs
 Medicare Savings Programs, run through your state and overseen by the Centers
 for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), help pay Medicare premiums and sometimes
 deductibles and copays. There are four tiers, each with its own income and
 resource limits for 2026:
 Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB)
 Income limits are $1,350 a month for an individual and $1,824 a month for a
 couple. QMB covers Part A and Part B premiums plus deductibles, coinsurance, and
 copays.
 Specified Low-Income Medicare Beneficiary (SLMB)
 Income limits are $1,616 a month for an individual and $2,184 a month for a
 couple. SLMB covers Part B premiums.
 Qualifying Individual (QI)
 Income limits are $1,816 a month for an individual and $2,455 a month for a
 couple. QI covers Part B premiums.
 Qualified Disabled and Working Individuals (QDWI)
 Income limits are $5,405 a month for an individual and $7,299 a month for a
 couple. QDWI covers Part A premiums only.
 Advertisement
 The resource limit for QMB, SLMB, and QI is $9,950 for an individual and $14,910
 for a couple; QDWI's resource limit is $4,000 for an individual and $6,000 for a
 couple, per CMS. Some states don't count resources at all or use higher income
 thresholds, so it's worth applying even if you think you're over the limit.
 Contact your state Medicaid office to apply.
 3. Supplemental Security Income for very low income and resources
 Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a separate federal program from Social
 Security retirement benefits, run by the SSA for people 65 or older, or of any
 age if blind or disabled, who have limited income and resources. The federal
 payment standard for 2026 is $994 a month for an individual and $1,491 for a
 couple, though some states add a supplement on top. To qualify, an individual
 generally needs unearned income under $1,014 a month, and a couple under $1,511
 a month, per SSA figures. Resource limits are $2,000 for an individual and
 $3,000 for a couple, and resources generally don't include your home, one
 vehicle, or burial funds. If you receive Social Security retirement or survivor
 benefits as your only income and that amount is low enough, you could
 potentially also qualify for a reduced SSI payment. Apply through your local SSA
 office.
 Save Money: Things to cut when living on retirement (many people ignore #11) 
 4. SNAP food assistance
 The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), administered by the U.S.
 Department of Agriculture (USDA) through state agencies, helps eligible
 households buy groceries. Income limits vary by household size and are adjusted
 annually, so check the USDA's SNAP eligibility tool or your state agency for
 current figures. Households with a member age 60 or older, or one receiving
 disability benefits, only need to meet a net income test and can deduct
 out-of-pocket medical expenses over $35 a month, per USDA rules. If everyone in
 the household already receives SSI or TANF, the household may be automatically
 considered income-eligible for SNAP. In California, SSI recipients can apply for
 CalFresh (the state's SNAP program) directly through a Social Security office
 under certain conditions, per SSA guidance.
 5. LIHEAP help with utility bills
 The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), funded by the U.S.
 Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and administered by states, helps
 eligible households pay heating and cooling bills. Under federal rules, no
 household can be excluded if its income falls below 110% of the federal poverty
 guidelines, though states have discretion to set their own thresholds and may use different standards from year to year. If you already
 receive SNAP or Medicaid, you may automatically meet LIHEAP's income test in
 many states. LIHEAP funds are limited and distributed through state and local
 agencies, so applying early in the season can matter. Contact your state's
 LIHEAP office or local community action agency to apply.
 6. Housing assistance through HUD programs
 The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) oversees several
 programs that can reduce housing costs for low-income older adults, including
 Housing Choice Vouchers (commonly known as Section 8) and public housing. These
 programs generally base eligibility on local area median income limits, which
 vary significantly by city and county, and are set and updated by HUD. Because
 voucher waiting lists can run long in many areas, applying as soon as you know
 your income qualifies may help, even if you don't need assistance immediately.
 Contact your local public housing agency to check local income limits and
 application timelines.
 Retire like the rich: 14 ways you could build wealth in your 50s. 
 7. State-specific supplemental programs
 Beyond federal programs, many states layer on their own assistance. Some states
 add a supplement to the federal SSI payment, which means the actual combined
 benefit can be higher than the $994 individual or $1,491 couple federal floor,
 depending on where you live and your living arrangement, according to SSA data.
 States also administer their own property tax relief programs for seniors,
 state-funded pharmacy assistance programs, and expanded Medicaid eligibility
 pathways. Because these vary so much by state, checking with your state's
 department of aging or human services office is the most reliable way to find
 out what's available locally.
 Bottom line
 Living on Social Security alone doesn't automatically qualify you for any of
 these programs, but it also doesn't disqualify you. Each program has its own
 income and resource tests, and many people who assume they earn "too much" turn
 out to be eligible, especially once housing costs, medical expenses, or
 state-specific rules are factored in.
 The SSA, CMS, and USDA all offer free screening tools and local office contacts
 that can help you check your
 eligibility across multiple programs at once, rather than applying one by
 one and guessing. Setting up a my Social Security account online can also help
 you track your current benefit amount and COLA notices, which many of these
 programs ask for during the application process.
